quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: Rice is one of the few major crops that can grow in flooded fields. Farmers often flood the paddies because standing water keeps weeds from sprouting and provides steady moisture. However, this method also creates conditions in which bacteria release methane, a gas that contributes to warming. Researchers have found that letting the fields dry out briefly during the growing season can reduce these emissions by about a third. Yields usually stay the same, provided that the drying period is timed carefully. Adoption has been slow because farmers fear losing part of their harvest. Some governments now pay farmers who adopt the drier method.
quests.question: Careful timing matters if farmers want to dry their paddies without losing yield.
quests.hint: Look for the condition attached to stable yields.
quests.explanation: Yields usually stay the same provided the drying period is timed carefully.
quests.evidenceLine: Yields usually stay the same, provided that the drying period is timed carefully.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: Two friends, Renee and Tobias, each invested $1,000 at the beginning of the year. Renee chose a fund that gained twenty percent in the first six months and lost twenty percent in the second half. Tobias chose a fund that gained nothing but lost nothing either. Many people assume that Renee ended up exactly where she began, since twenty percent up and twenty percent down seems to cancel out. In fact, she finished with $960, because the second loss was calculated on a larger amount. Tobias's account still held exactly $1,000. Financial advisers use this example to warn against judging funds by simple averages.
quests.question: Tobias ended the year with more money than Renee.
quests.hint: Compare the two final balances.
quests.explanation: Renee finished with $960 and Tobias with $1,000.
quests.evidenceLine: In fact, she finished with $960, because the second loss was calculated on a larger amount. Tobias's account still held exactly $1,000.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: When a language has no word for a concept, speakers usually borrow one from another language. English has done this so often that it now contains words from more than a hundred languages. "Shampoo" comes from Hindi, "kindergarten" from German, and "ketchup" from a Chinese dialect. Some purists resist borrowing, believing that a language should draw on its own resources. Others argue that borrowing is a sign of a healthy, living language. Linguists generally note that no major language has ever remained entirely free of foreign words. New words enter dictionaries every year after appearing frequently in print.
quests.question: Every major language has borrowed at least some foreign words.
quests.hint: Read what linguists generally note.
quests.explanation: No major language has stayed entirely free of foreign words, so all have borrowed some.
quests.evidenceLine: Linguists generally note that no major language has ever remained entirely free of foreign words.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: In many societies, it is customary to remove one's hat when entering a church, while in synagogues men often keep one on. Such rules can seem contradictory to outsiders, but each is a sign of respect within its own tradition. Visitors who are unsure of the custom are usually forgiven, provided they show curiosity and politeness. Guidebooks therefore often include short sections on etiquette. Locals tend to appreciate an honest question more than a silent mistake. The safest approach is to observe what others do and follow their lead. Tour operators often remind visitors about local dress rules before a trip.
quests.question: The two traditions show respect by requiring the same behavior with hats.
quests.hint: Compare the hat customs in the two places.
quests.explanation: One removes hats and the other often keeps them on, though both mean respect.
quests.evidenceLine: In many societies, it is customary to remove one's hat when entering a church, while in synagogues men often keep one on. Such rules can seem contradictory to outsiders, but each is a sign of respect within its own tradition.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: A recent survey found that ninety percent of people say they are concerned about climate change. However, only about a third said they had changed their habits, such as flying less or eating less meat. Psychologists call this the gap between attitudes and behavior. They suggest that individual action feels small compared with the size of the problem, which reduces motivation. Campaigns that show concrete local benefits, such as cleaner air, tend to be more effective. Making the greener choice the easy default helps as well. Researchers also find that people copy the habits of friends and neighbors.
quests.question: Most people who worry about climate change have altered their habits.
quests.hint: Compare the two survey figures.
quests.explanation: Only about a third have changed their habits, so most have not.
quests.evidenceLine: However, only about a third said they had changed their habits, such as flying less or eating less meat.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: Ingrid had been managing the warehouse for ten years when the company introduced a new inventory system. At first, she resisted it, believing that her own methods were faster. After a month, however, she noticed that errors had dropped and that she could find products in half the time. She asked to lead the training for her colleagues. Now she says that the change taught her not to confuse experience with the best possible method. Her manager has since promoted her. Her colleagues now ask her for advice about other changes.
quests.question: Ingrid's opinion of the new system shifted once she saw the results.
quests.hint: Compare her first reaction with what she noticed later.
quests.explanation: She resisted at first but later saw fewer errors and faster searches, and she asked to lead the training.
quests.evidenceLine: After a month, however, she noticed that errors had dropped and that she could find products in half the time.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: Many people assume that brown sugar is healthier than white sugar. Brown sugar is simply white sugar with a small amount of molasses added, which gives it color and a slightly richer flavor. The mineral content of the molasses is too small to have any noticeable health effect. Nutritionists therefore treat both types in the same way, as sweeteners that should be limited. Chefs, on the other hand, choose between them for taste and texture. Cookies made with brown sugar tend to be softer and chewier. Many cooks keep both kinds in the cupboard.
quests.question: Nutritionists see brown sugar as a healthy alternative to white sugar.
quests.hint: How do nutritionists treat the two types?
quests.explanation: They treat both alike, as sweeteners to be limited.
quests.evidenceLine: Nutritionists therefore treat both types in the same way, as sweeteners that should be limited.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: Meteorologists distinguish between weather and climate. Weather describes conditions on a particular day, such as rain in the afternoon or a cold morning. Climate refers to the average of these conditions over decades. A single unusually cold winter therefore does not disprove that the planet is warming. Similarly, a hot summer is not proof by itself. Scientists look at long records collected across many regions to identify trends. News reports often confuse the two ideas.
quests.question: One cold winter is not enough to show that the planet is not warming.
quests.hint: Ask how long a period climate is measured over.
quests.explanation: Climate is an average over decades, so one winter cannot disprove warming.
quests.evidenceLine: A single unusually cold winter therefore does not disprove that the planet is warming.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: The school's new grading system replaces letter grades with written comments. Teachers describe what each student does well and what needs improvement, and no scores are given. Supporters say that this encourages students to focus on learning instead of competing. Critics worry that universities and employers will find the comments hard to compare. The school has therefore agreed to provide a summary sheet for students applying elsewhere. The system will be reviewed after two years. Parents were invited to a meeting to ask questions.
quests.question: Students who apply elsewhere will get a summary sheet.
quests.hint: Find the school's response to the critics.
quests.explanation: The school agreed to provide a summary sheet for those applying elsewhere.
quests.evidenceLine: The school has therefore agreed to provide a summary sheet for students applying elsewhere.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: A small software company doubled its number of customers in a year, but its profits fell. The reason was that the company offered a very low price to attract users, and it spent heavily on support. Once customers had joined, it became clear that many would leave if prices rose. The founders decided to keep the low price and reduce costs by simplifying the product. Profits recovered slowly over the next year. They say they would have been wiser to test the price earlier. Their story is now taught in a local business course.
quests.question: Profits fell because the company had too few customers.
quests.hint: Read the first sentence for the trend in customers.
quests.explanation: The customer base doubled, so the problem was low prices and heavy support costs.
quests.evidenceLine: A small software company doubled its number of customers in a year, but its profits fell. The reason was that the company offered a very low price to attract users, and it spent heavily on support.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: Travelers often assume that the cheapest flight is always the best choice. However, low-cost airlines frequently charge extra for baggage, seat selection, and even printing a boarding pass. A ticket that looks fifty dollars cheaper can end up costing more than a full-service fare. Comparing the final price, including all fees, is therefore essential. Some comparison websites now show the total cost from the start. Passengers who travel with only a small bag can still benefit from low-cost carriers. Travel writers often advise reading the fine print carefully.
quests.question: A budget ticket is guaranteed to cost less than a full-service fare.
quests.hint: What can happen once extra fees are added?
quests.explanation: A ticket that looks cheaper can end up costing more, so no saving is guaranteed.
quests.evidenceLine: A ticket that looks fifty dollars cheaper can end up costing more than a full-service fare.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: In the last kilometers of a cycling race, the leaders often slow down and watch each other. Because the rider at the front takes the most wind, no one wants to lead. This cautious phase can allow riders from behind to catch up. Then a sudden attack from one rider forces everyone to accelerate. The winner is often the one who has saved energy earlier. Commentators describe these moments as a game of nerves. Team managers usually shout instructions from a car behind the group.
quests.question: Riders are eager to take the front position in the final kilometers.
quests.hint: Why is the front position unpopular?
quests.explanation: The front rider takes the most wind, so nobody wants to lead.
quests.evidenceLine: Because the rider at the front takes the most wind, no one wants to lead.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: Carbon monoxide is dangerous because it has no smell, color, or taste. It is produced when fuels such as gas, oil, or wood burn without enough air. In small amounts, it can cause headaches and dizziness that people mistake for the flu. In larger amounts, it can be fatal within hours. Detectors that sound an alarm are therefore recommended in any home with a gas boiler or a fireplace. Alarms should be tested regularly and replaced according to the maker's instructions. Fire departments often check alarms for free during safety campaigns.
quests.question: Early symptoms of carbon monoxide poisoning can be confused with the flu.
quests.hint: Read what small amounts can cause.
quests.explanation: Headaches and dizziness that people mistake for the flu.
quests.evidenceLine: In small amounts, it can cause headaches and dizziness that people mistake for the flu.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: Many cities are experimenting with digital tools to manage traffic. Sensors at intersections count vehicles and adjust the timing of traffic lights in real time. In one pilot project, average waiting times fell by about fifteen percent during rush hour. However, the system worked best on main roads and made little difference in narrow side streets. Officials say that improving public transport would reduce congestion more than any timing system. The city will nevertheless extend the pilot to two more districts. Drivers can also see delays on a public map.
quests.question: The timing system helped mainly on the main roads.
quests.hint: Look for the "however" sentence.
quests.explanation: It worked best on main roads and made little difference on narrow side streets.
quests.evidenceLine: However, the system worked best on main roads and made little difference in narrow side streets.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: A shop advertises a jacket at 30 percent off the original price of $120. The next week, it offers a further 10 percent off the sale price for customers who sign up to its newsletter. Some shoppers assume this equals a 40 percent discount. In fact, the second discount applies to the already reduced price of $84, giving a final price of $75.60. The total reduction is therefore 37 percent, not 40 percent. Understanding this helps consumers judge whether a promotion is really a bargain. Store staff say that many customers ask them to explain the calculation.
quests.question: The two discounts together reduce the price by less than 40 percent.
quests.hint: Compare the total reduction with the shoppers' assumption.
quests.explanation: The passage calculates a total reduction of 37 percent, which is below 40.
quests.evidenceLine: The total reduction is therefore 37 percent, not 40 percent.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: Some people think that muscle turns into fat when they stop exercising. In reality, these are two different tissues, and one cannot change into the other. What happens is that muscle shrinks when it is not used, while fat can accumulate if a person continues to eat the same amount. The body may therefore look softer, even though the tissues are the same ones that were always there. Regular resistance exercise can rebuild lost muscle, although it takes time. Older adults are advised to keep active for this reason. Doctors say that healthy sleep supports muscle growth as well.
quests.question: Muscle tissue gradually changes into fat when a person becomes inactive.
quests.hint: Can one tissue become the other?
quests.explanation: The passage says they are different tissues and one cannot change into the other.
quests.evidenceLine: In reality, these are two different tissues, and one cannot change into the other.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: A film score is not merely background music. Composers plan when the music should enter and when silence would be more effective. In some famous scenes, the absence of music is what creates tension. Directors often play the same scene with different music to see how the audience's feelings change. The results can be dramatic: a peaceful garden can seem threatening with a low, slow tune. Some viewers do not consciously notice the music but are strongly affected by it. Sound designers work closely with composers on such scenes.
quests.question: The same scene can produce different feelings depending on the music.
quests.hint: What do directors test with the same scene?
quests.explanation: A peaceful garden can seem threatening with a low, slow tune.
quests.evidenceLine: Directors often play the same scene with different music to see how the audience's feelings change. The results can be dramatic: a peaceful garden can seem threatening with a low, slow tune.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: The idea of a "gap year" between school and university is popular in Britain and Australia, where many young people work or travel for a year. In some countries, however, it is uncommon, and students who delay their studies may be seen as lacking ambition. Supporters of gap years argue that they improve maturity and help students choose a subject more wisely. Studies suggest that students who take a year off often perform slightly better at university. Critics worry that some never return to education. The practice is therefore judged differently from place to place. Universities in both countries publish advice for students planning a year off.
quests.question: Students who take a gap year usually perform worse at university.
quests.hint: What do the studies suggest about performance?
quests.explanation: They suggest such students often perform slightly better, not worse.
quests.evidenceLine: Studies suggest that students who take a year off often perform slightly better at university.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: Mangrove forests grow along tropical coastlines, where their roots stand in salty water. Their dense roots slow the waves and trap sand and mud, which protects the shore from erosion. During storms, coastal villages behind mangroves suffer less damage than those without them. Despite this, mangroves have been cleared in many places to make room for shrimp farms. The shrimp farms often become unproductive after a few years, and the protection is lost. Some communities are now replanting mangroves by hand. Local fishermen say the fish have also returned to the replanted areas.
quests.question: Villages sheltered by mangroves usually suffer less storm damage.
quests.hint: Compare villages with and without mangroves.
quests.explanation: Villages behind mangroves suffer less damage during storms.
quests.evidenceLine: During storms, coastal villages behind mangroves suffer less damage than those without them.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: Migratory monarch butterflies fly thousands of kilometers from North America to central Mexico each autumn. No individual butterfly makes the whole round trip, since the journey north takes several generations. The butterflies that fly south in autumn live much longer than those born in summer. Scientists are still investigating how these insects know where to go, since none has made the journey before. Loss of milkweed plants, the only food of the caterpillars, is one of the main threats. Gardeners are being encouraged to plant milkweed. Volunteers tag butterflies with tiny stickers to follow their journeys.
quests.question: The butterflies that reach Mexico have never made the trip before.
quests.hint: Notice why the scientists find the navigation puzzling.
quests.explanation: None has made the journey before, which is why its navigation is a mystery.
quests.evidenceLine: Scientists are still investigating how these insects know where to go, since none has made the journey before.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: Many people believe that they work best when they multitask. Research suggests otherwise: switching between tasks costs time, because the brain needs a moment to refocus each time. People who frequently switch also tend to make more mistakes and remember less. A better approach is to work in focused blocks of twenty-five to fifty minutes, followed by a short break. Turning off notifications during these blocks makes them more effective. Many workers find that they finish sooner this way. Software companies now sell apps that block distracting websites.
quests.question: Research shows that switching between tasks saves people time.
quests.hint: What does research say about switching?
quests.explanation: Switching costs time, so it does not save any.
quests.evidenceLine: Research suggests otherwise: switching between tasks costs time, because the brain needs a moment to refocus each time.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: When a website asks whether you accept cookies, it is referring to small files stored on your device. Some cookies are useful, for example by keeping items in your shopping basket. Others track which pages you visit so that advertisers can show you related products. Laws in Europe require sites to ask for permission before using tracking cookies. Many users click "accept" without reading, simply to remove the message. Privacy groups say that this weakens the purpose of the law. Some browsers now let users block tracking cookies with one setting.
quests.question: Some cookies record which pages people visit so advertisers can target them.
quests.hint: Find the sentence that begins with "Others."
quests.explanation: Tracking cookies note the pages you visit so that advertisers can show related products.
quests.evidenceLine: Others track which pages you visit so that advertisers can show you related products.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: A well-known news agency changed its rules for reporting on public opinion polls. From now on, reporters must state the sample size and the margin of error in every story. Editors say that without these details, readers may think a small difference between two candidates is meaningful. In many cases, the gap lies within the margin of error and could be the result of chance. The new policy has been criticized by a few reporters for making stories longer. Overall, reader feedback has been positive. Similar rules already exist at several other agencies.
quests.question: Reporters may skip the margin of error when a story is short.
quests.hint: What must reporters state in every story?
quests.explanation: Both the sample size and the margin of error are required in every story.
quests.evidenceLine: From now on, reporters must state the sample size and the margin of error in every story.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: Translators sometimes face the problem of words that have no direct equivalent. In Japanese, the word "komorebi" describes sunlight filtering through the leaves of trees. English has no single word for this, so translators must use a phrase. Some argue that such words show that speakers of a language notice different things. Others believe that people everywhere notice the same things but simply lack a name for them. The debate has continued for decades without a clear answer. Language teachers often use such words to spark discussion.
quests.question: Translating komorebi into English takes more than one word.
quests.hint: Look at what translators must use.
quests.explanation: English has no single word, so a phrase is needed.
quests.evidenceLine: English has no single word for this, so translators must use a phrase.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: In tennis, a player who wins the first set has a clear advantage, but the match is far from over. Statistics show that about one in four players who lose the first set still win the match. Comebacks are more common in men's tournaments, where matches can last five sets. Fitness matters greatly in long matches, and players with better endurance can recover after a bad start. Coaches therefore advise their players never to give up early. Many memorable victories began with a lost set. Sports psychologists teach players to treat each point as a new start.
quests.question: Players who lose the opening set win the match fewer than one time in ten.
quests.hint: Turn "one in four" into a percentage.
quests.explanation: One in four is 25 percent, which is far more than one in ten.
quests.evidenceLine: Statistics show that about one in four players who lose the first set still win the match.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: Painting the ceiling white is often recommended because white reflects more light than darker colors. However, in a room with little daylight, a light color can make the space feel flat and cold. Some designers suggest using a warm shade instead, such as soft cream or pale yellow. It is important to test the color on a small area and watch how it changes during the day. Paint that looks pleasant in the shop may look very different under home lighting. Samples are usually inexpensive. Local shops often let customers borrow sample pots for a few days.
quests.question: Designers say a white ceiling works well in dim rooms too.
quests.hint: What does the "however" sentence say about dim rooms?
quests.explanation: A light color can feel flat and cold in a room with little daylight, and warm shades are suggested.
quests.evidenceLine: However, in a room with little daylight, a light color can make the space feel flat and cold. Some designers suggest using a warm shade instead, such as soft cream or pale yellow.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: Older people often say that families used to eat dinner together every night, but the reality was more complicated. Historians point out that in many working-class households, fathers worked late and children ate earlier. Regular family meals were more typical of middle-class homes during the 1950s. Today, studies show that families who eat together several times a week tend to communicate better. The benefit, however, seems to come from the conversation rather than from the food. Even a short shared meal can help. Sociologists continue to study how meal habits are changing.
quests.question: Historians say that shared dinners were normal in every household in the past.
quests.hint: Whose households are said to have eaten separately?
quests.explanation: In many working-class households, fathers worked late and children ate earlier.
quests.evidenceLine: Historians point out that in many working-class households, fathers worked late and children ate earlier. Regular family meals were more typical of middle-class homes during the 1950s.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: A bakery discovered that it was throwing away almost a quarter of its bread each day. The owner began giving unsold loaves to a local shelter at closing time. Later, she introduced a discount for bread bought after 6 p.m., and sales during the evening increased noticeably. Waste dropped to less than five percent within three months. Customers say they appreciate the lower prices as well as the environmental benefit. The owner has now been asked to advise other shops. She has also started a small blog about her methods.
quests.question: Discounting evening bread helped the bakery cut its waste.
quests.hint: Connect the discount with the drop in waste.
quests.explanation: Evening sales rose after the discount, and waste fell below five percent.
quests.evidenceLine: Later, she introduced a discount for bread bought after 6 p.m., and sales during the evening increased noticeably. Waste dropped to less than five percent within three months.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: Scientists once believed that the Sun revolved around the Earth, but observations gradually showed otherwise. In the sixteenth century, Copernicus proposed that the planets, including Earth, orbit the Sun. His idea was not immediately accepted, because it seemed to contradict everyday experience and religious teachings. Later, Galileo's telescope revealed moons circling Jupiter, which showed that not everything orbits Earth. Over time, measurements became precise enough to settle the question. Today the Sun-centered model is a basic part of astronomy. Textbooks often use this episode to explain how science changes.
quests.question: Copernicus's proposal was quickly accepted by most people.
quests.hint: How was the idea received at first?
quests.explanation: It was not immediately accepted, because it seemed to contradict experience and religion.
quests.evidenceLine: His idea was not immediately accepted, because it seemed to contradict everyday experience and religious teachings.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the passage.
quests.passage: At the start of the term, Mr. Okafor asked his students to write a letter to themselves about their goals. He collected the letters and promised to return them at the end of the year. Many students forgot what they had written, and some were surprised by how their goals had changed. Others discovered that they had achieved more than they expected. Mr. Okafor says that the exercise helps students to notice their own progress. He plans to repeat it next year. Some students said they wanted to keep the letters forever.
quests.question: The students read their letters again a few weeks after writing them.
quests.hint: When were the letters returned?
quests.explanation: At the end of the year, not after a few weeks.
quests.evidenceLine: He collected the letters and promised to return them at the end of the year.
